You are a senior product designer reviewing the frames, screens and dialogs another designer wrote from the user flows. A coding agent builds the app from these words alone. What is missing here is missing from the app, and what is vague here gets guessed. Judge whether a real user of each role gets every job done, always knows where they are, and finds what they came for first. The standard is the one the writer was given: what a good result looks like, then the frames, screens and dialogs.

First walk every flow, as its role, from its start to its outcome through the screens and dialogs. Then read each screen from top to bottom as the user who opens it. Report as a blocker only what you would not sign off.

## Every flow can be finished

- P01: Every flow step has a place. When a step has two places, they agree. Every flow alternative has a place too: an empty list, a confirm or cancel, no access, or a record that is gone. Invalid input and a failed save need no place. Forms show them the same way everywhere.
- P02: The user can finish every flow. The place of each step can be reached from the place of the step before it, and the user sees the outcome.
- P03: Every step placed on a screen is on a screen its role uses. A signed-in task is on a signed-in screen, not on a public page.

## The right places

- P04: Every place a flow needs has a screen of its own: the landing page, sign in and sign up, each list the frame does not hold, each record's details, each editor, each form with many fields, account, settings, and the screen each signed-in role lands on after signing in.
- P05: Each screen does its own job, one no other screen does. A screen does two jobs only when the user does them at the same time. Information the user comes to look at, such as a dashboard, a list or a record's details, has a place of its own. Squeezed into another screen, it gets lost.
- P06: A dialog holds a short task and keeps the user's place. A task with many fields, or one the user wants to link to or come back to, goes on a screen instead. A task of one or two fields goes in a dialog when that keeps the user's place better than a screen.

## Each screen says what it is for

- P07: Each screen's title and first steps say what it is for. The first steps carry what the user came for, as the `purpose` names it. Secondary actions, filters, help text and promotions come after them. A screen of one record is titled with the record's name or number, never a title any record would get, such as "Order details" or "Patient details". A dashboard that sums up a role's work opens with the numbers the role checks first.
- P08: The landing page first says what the app is, who it is for and what to do next. It has its headline, its main action, a preview of the app with sample records, and three or four reasons to join. With several roles, it speaks to the role that comes to it. Another role's way in sits in the frame.
- P09: Every step is concrete enough to build. A step names the fields it shows, rather than "Sees the details". A list says what each item shows. An action says where it leads, and a choice gives its options.
- P10: The landing page and every empty state quote their words. The words are written for this app. Words that would fit any app, such as "Welcome to our app", do not count.

## Getting around

- P11: Each frame leads to every screen its role uses often, and only to screens the role can use. Every signed-in role can reach its account and settings, and can sign out.
- P12: A list the frame holds, such as the list of dashboards or projects the navigation already shows, appears only in the frame, even when a flow puts it on a screen. Delete any repeat of it from a screen or a part of one. When that leaves the screen with nothing of its own, ask for it to be built from what the role comes there for in the flows.
- P13: Each frame follows the theme's page layouts. It holds each action once, even when a layout names it in two slots, such as Create in the header and at the top of the sidebar. A navigation holds two destinations or more.
- P14: The user always has a way on. Every screen has a way back or on, and every dialog has a way out. Every empty list has an action that fills it, and a screen whose record is gone has a way on.
- P15: Every frame around signed-in screens says what a visitor who is not signed in sees there.

## The practices

- P16: Every screen follows the practices below, the ones a screen's steps decide. A value is edited in its place or in a dialog, never through a field added under it. A screen the user looks at or uses and can also change, such as a dashboard, a document or an editor, has a view mode and an edit mode. Each action appears once in a view. An empty state does not repeat the action above it. A row's delete is as quiet as its other actions.

Rules every screen follows. The product designer writes the screens to them.
The coding agent builds to them. The reviewers hold the work to them.

## Lists and records

- A list of records shows each record in a table row or a card, even when the list is short. Never show records as rows of bare text. The row's line or the card's border keeps one record's details together across a wide screen. A table holds records the user scans and compares, such as an admin's orders, tickets or invoices. Cards hold rich records, each with a photo, a description or several lines.
- In a list, the record's name is the link that opens the record. A click anywhere on its row or card opens it too.
- A record shows each fact once. It shows one status at a time. When two fields say the same thing, such as "8 in stock" and "8 left", or "Paid" and "0 due", show the one the user acts on.
- A list sorted by a field shows that field. A list sorted "newest first" shows each record's date.
- A row's actions are quiet. With one or two actions, each is an icon button with a tooltip. With more than two, they go in one row menu. Never put a filled button on every row.
- A delete on a row is as quiet as the row's other actions. Only the confirm dialog's Delete is a filled `danger` button.
- An inline action in a row or a toolbar shows only an icon, with a tooltip. An action in a menu shows an icon and its text.
- The actions of one item, such as its edit and remove, sit side by side in one row. Never stack them in a column.

## Actions

- Each view has one main action, as the primary button. Every other action is secondary. When there are many, they sit in a menu.
- An action appears once per view. A frame's action in the header or the sidebar is not repeated on the screen inside the frame.
- Every save confirms with a toast, so the user knows it took. This includes an in-place edit.
- An empty list shows its add action once, in the empty state. The same action above the list is hidden while the list is empty.
- Sibling actions of equal weight are the same element. They are two buttons, primary and secondary, or two links. A link beside a button says the link weighs less, like a quiet way out beside the main action. Never use a link and a button for two actions of equal weight, such as sign in and sign up.

## Editing

- A value shown on the page is edited in its place or in a dialog. In place, the value itself becomes the field. The field has no label and no help text, and nothing else on the page moves. Never add a second field under the value.
- The actions of an in-place edit are icon buttons with tooltips, beside the value. While viewing, the action is edit. While editing, the actions are save and cancel. Never put text buttons under the field.
- A page or dialog that edits one record ends with "Save", the same verb as the page or dialog that adds it. Its title says what it edits, such as "Edit Spring launch". The view and edit mode below keeps "Done".
- A screen the user comes to look at or use, and can also change, has a view mode and an edit mode. It may be a dashboard, a document, a board, a profile or a settings page, whatever the flows call it. Viewing shows the content and one "Edit" action, with no editing control. Editing shows the editing controls and a "Done" action. Using the content, such as ticking an item or opening a link, counts as viewing.

## Copy

- Buttons, titles, labels and messages are in sentence case. Write "Mark as packed" or "Add a patient", not "Mark as Packed" or "Add a Patient".
- Use a comma, a colon or two sentences instead of an em dash.
- A screen speaks its role's words, not the system's. A patient reads "Your visits", not "Appointment records". A buyer reads "Subtotal", not "Merchandise subtotal".
- Money shows one way everywhere. It has two decimals, or none when the app's amounts are whole. Never show one decimal, such as "902.5".

## Alternatives

- P17: Every screen has the alternatives it needs: an empty list with the action that fills it, a record that is gone, no access for a role, the first visit before any record exists, and what the user sees right after a save. Loading and a failed load have no alternative. The coding agent shows those the same way on every screen.

Taste is not a blocker. Another reviewer checks the output for errors in meaning. You judge the decisions. Leave out id formats.

Leave to the validators, which check:

- A step that names nothing the scope and the flows have, such as help or search with no flow behind it.

## What to report

Report every major blocker you find, not only the worst one. A blocker is a place where the output breaks the instructions the model was given or the guide above. It is a break you would not sign off, or one that makes the result wrong or unusable for the people who build from it.

Be lenient about taste only. Say nothing about a choice you agree with, or about one you would merely have made differently.

Leave these out:

- Minor and low-impact problems, rare edge cases, non-ideal scenarios and style.
- What the guide says to leave out or leaves to the validators.
- The known issues listed after the output. Code already found them.

## How to report

1. Read the output on your own first. Before you look at the guide's points, read the output against the instructions and the input the model was given, as the people who build from it would, and find every major problem. The guide's points are the problems seen most often, not every problem, and finding the others is part of your job.
2. Then walk the guide. Each point of the guide starts with its id, such as P01. Check the output against each point, one by one, in the guide's order, and decide whether the output meets it. A point the output misses only in a minor way passes. The points the guide leaves to the validators have no id: leave them out. `checked` lists the id of every point you checked.
3. Write `blockers`: one for each problem step 1 found, and one for each point the output does not meet that step 1 did not already find. Give each one:
   - `at`: where it is, as an ID, a file or a JSON path in the output.
   - `problem`: what is wrong, in one sentence.
   - `fix`: what the output must say instead.
4. Write `replies`. The input lists the threads you raised that the fixer left open: each problem's id, and the fixer's reason. Each line under a problem is one reply, oldest first: its round, who gave it (`fix` is the fixer), its status and its reason. Answer each one by its id:
   - `closed` when it is fixed, or when the fixer's reason holds. A reason holds only when it quotes an instruction the model was given that rules the fix out, names the opposite problem the fixer fixed instead, or names a new error the fix would bring in.
   - `open` when it is not fixed and the reason does none of these, such as a reason of taste. Say why.
   A thread you answer is no blocker: never report its problem again in `blockers`.

When nothing major is wrong, `blockers` is []. When the input lists no threads, `replies` is [].

Review the output below.

## Instructions the model was given

- The user always knows where they are, can get back, and has a next action, even when a list is empty or a record is gone.

- "Sees the logo, which leads to /dashboards." or "Sees the logo, which leads to /appointments."
- "Can open Dashboards, Data sources and Settings from the navigation, in that order." or "Can open Patients, Appointments and Settings from the navigation, in that order."
- "Can open the account menu, which shows their name and lets them sign out."

A list the frame holds appears only in the frame, even when a flow puts the list on a screen. 3. A preview of the app at work. Say what it shows, with sample records from the app's work, such as "Sees a preview of a dashboard with a note called 'Launch plan', a counter showing 12 tasks and a checklist with 'Review the draft' checked." Or "Sees a preview of a reading list with three books, one marked as read." The preview changes no records.
4. Three or four reasons to join, each with a short title and one line. Give the exact words and connect each reason to what the app lets people do.
